section.title: God of Vengeance, Shine Forth
section.sectionRationale: A communal lament crying out to the God of vengeance against the arrogant who oppress the vulnerable and mock God's sight, this psalm moves from urgent protest to confident trust, resting in the LORD as stronghold and rock of refuge, the very justice ultimately entrusted to Christ, the appointed Judge.
section.thesis: The psalmist cries to the God of vengeance to rise up as Judge against the wicked who crush the weak and mock God's awareness, and finds settled confidence that the LORD, who disciplines and never forsakes His own, will turn the wickedness of the wicked back upon themselves.
section.frameNote: Six movements: an urgent cry to the Judge of the earth, verses 1-3; a portrait of the arrogant wicked, verses 4-7; a rebuke of the foolish who doubt God sees, verses 8-11; the blessing of divine discipline and certain justice, verses 12-15; a personal testimony of God's help, verses 16-19; and confidence in God as the final Judge, verses 20-23.

units.label: Rise Up, O Judge of the Earth

verses.text: O LORD, God of {{naqam|vengeance}}, O God of vengeance, shine forth.
Rise up, O Judge of the earth; render a reward to the proud.
How long will the wicked, O LORD, how long will the wicked exult?

units.label: They Crush Your People
units.note: a portrait of the arrogant wicked

verses.text: They pour out arrogant words; all workers of iniquity boast.
They crush Your people, O LORD; they oppress Your heritage.
They kill the widow and the foreigner; they murder the fatherless.
They say, "The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob pays no heed."

units.label: He Who Formed the Eye, Can He Not See

verses.text: Take notice, O senseless among the people! O fools, when will you be wise?
He who affixed the ear, can He not hear? He who formed the eye, can He not see?
He who admonishes the nations, does He not discipline? He who teaches man, does He lack knowledge?
The LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are futile.

units.label: Blessed Is the Man You Discipline
units.note: the blessing of discipline and certain justice

verses.text: Blessed is the man You {{yasar|discipline}}, O LORD, and teach from Your law,
to grant him relief from days of trouble, until a pit is dug for the wicked.
For the LORD will not forsake His people; He will never abandon His heritage.
Surely {{mishpat|judgment}} will again be righteous, and all the upright in heart will follow it.

units.label: Your Loving Devotion Supports Me
units.note: a personal testimony of God's help

verses.text: Who will rise up for me against the wicked? Who will stand for me against the workers of iniquity?
Unless the LORD had been my helper, I would soon have dwelt in the abode of silence.
If I say, "My foot is slipping," Your loving devotion, O LORD, supports me.
When anxiety overwhelms me, Your consolation delights my soul.

units.label: The Lord Is My Rock of Refuge

verses.text: Can a corrupt throne be Your ally, one devising mischief by decree?
They band together against the righteous and condemn the innocent to death.
But the LORD has been my {{misgab|stronghold}}, and my God is my rock of refuge.
He will bring upon them their own iniquity and destroy them for their wickedness. The LORD our God will destroy them.

naqam.gloss: Vengeance, just retribution for wrong done. The psalmist appeals to this quality of God not as personal revenge but as the righteous judgment only the sovereign Judge of the earth may rightly execute.

yasar.gloss: To discipline, correct, or instruct. God's discipline of His own people is presented here as a blessing, distinct from His judgment on the unrepentant wicked, since it is aimed at teaching and relief, not destruction.

mishpat.gloss: Judgment, justice, the exercise of righteous legal decision. The psalmist trusts that this quality of God's rule will again prevail, however delayed it may currently seem.

misgab.gloss: A stronghold, a high, secure place of defense. The psalm closes by naming the LORD Himself this stronghold, the settled ground of confidence even while corrupt human power seems to prevail.

basic.context: The psalmist cries out to the God of vengeance against arrogant oppressors who crush the vulnerable, the widow, the foreigner, and the fatherless, and who mock God's very awareness of their crimes. The psalm moves from urgent protest to settled trust that the LORD disciplines but never abandons His people, and will destroy the wicked in the end.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm describes a specific community's experience of injustice under corrupt power, and it prescribes an abiding pattern: bringing outrage over injustice honestly to God as the rightful Judge, rather than taking vengeance into human hands.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalmist appeals to the LORD as the God of naqam, vengeance, verse 1, distinguishing God's righteous yasar, discipline, of His own people, verse 12, from His judgment on the wicked. He trusts that mishpat, justice, verse 15, will prevail, and closes calling God his misgab, stronghold, verse 22.
basic.typology: The psalm's cry for God to rise up as Judge of the earth, and its confidence that He will not forsake His heritage, anticipates the New Testament's teaching that God has appointed a day when He will judge the world in righteousness through Christ.
basic.christ: God the Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son, John 5:22, so the vindication this psalm cries out for is entrusted fully to Jesus Christ. At the cross, apparent injustice, the condemnation of the truly innocent, was itself the means by which God's ultimate justice and mercy were accomplished, Acts 2:23-24.
basic.god: God is shown as the rightful avenger of injustice, the Judge of the earth who sees and hears everything, who lovingly disciplines His own people for their good, and who remains their stronghold and rock of refuge even while corrupt power seems, for a time, to prevail.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 12:19 teaches believers to leave vengeance to God rather than avenge themselves. Hebrews 12:6 affirms that the Lord disciplines the one He loves. John 5:22 shows the Father has entrusted all judgment to the Son.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's cry for the God of vengeance to shine forth and judge the wicked, and its confidence that God will never abandon His people, is answered fully in Christ, to whom the Father has given all judgment, and who at the cross turned apparent injustice into the very means of the world's redemption.

context.literary:
Psalm 94 keeps changing its audience, and the changes are the structure. Verses 1 to 7 speak to God in urgent imperatives, shine forth, rise up, render, and in a doubled 'How long.' Verses 8 to 11 swing round to address the people, and turn the psalmist's prayer into a rebuke of the fools who have said God does not see. Verses 12 to 15 speak of the blessed man in the third person, like a wisdom teacher. Verses 16 to 19 become a private testimony in the first person singular, and verses 20 to 23 return to God and to the enemy. The psalm is a lament and a wisdom poem braided together, and it moves the worshiper from shouting at the sky to sitting at a teacher's feet to telling his own story.

The opening and the close frame each other. The psalm begins by calling God 'God of vengeance' twice, and it ends by saying of the wicked that 'The LORD our God will destroy them,' a verb repeated for emphasis. The demand in verse 2, 'Rise up,' meets its rhetorical counterpart in verse 16, 'Who will rise up for me?' The psalmist looks round for a human champion, finds none, and the answer comes in verse 17: the LORD had been his helper.

The centre of the poem is the argument of verses 9 to 10, three questions that all expect the answer yes. Whoever fixed the ear hears, whoever formed the eye sees, whoever teaches the nations knows. It is one of the neatest pieces of reasoning in the Psalter, built on a single thought: the Maker cannot be less than His making.
context.historical:
The psalm carries no title in the Hebrew and no name of an author, so its date cannot be fixed from the text. Its world is one where the courts have failed. Verse 20 speaks of a throne 'devising mischief by decree,' and the word for decree is the ordinary word for a statute. The accusation is that law itself has been turned into a tool for harm, which is exactly what Isaiah denounces when he says 'Woe to those who enact unjust statutes and issue oppressive decrees,' Isaiah 10:1. Readers have placed it in the dark days of the monarchy, in the exile or in the troubled years after, and nothing in the wording settles the question.

What matters for the first hearers is the list of victims. The widow, the foreigner and the fatherless in verse 6 are the three groups Israel's law singled out for protection. God had said of them, 'You must not mistreat any widow or orphan. If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry,' Exodus 22:22-23, and Moses had said that He 'executes justice for the fatherless and widow, and He loves the foreigner,' Deuteronomy 10:18. Those who killed them were not only breaking human law but defying a word God had attached to His own name.

The mockery in verse 7 uses the short divine name, Yah, and the title 'God of Jacob,' which reminds the listener that this is the God who bound Himself to Israel by covenant. The oppressors have not merely said that no one is watching. They have said the covenant God is not. The Jewish tradition remembered the psalm in worship: the Mishnah records it as the psalm the Levites sang on the fourth day of the week, and the Greek Psalter carries the same note in its heading.
context.canonical:
Psalm 94 sits between the enthronement cry of Psalm 93, 'The LORD reigns,' and the call to worship of Psalm 95, and its position matters. If the LORD reigns, why do the wicked exult? Book IV of the Psalter opened after the shock of Psalm 89, where the covenant seemed to have failed, and these psalms teach a people without a king how to live under the kingship of God. Psalm 94 is the honest midpoint of that teaching, the place where the complaint is voiced before the praise resumes.

The phrase 'God of vengeance' reaches back to the Song of Moses. 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,' Deuteronomy 32:35, is followed at once by the promise that 'the LORD will vindicate His people and have compassion on His servants,' Deuteronomy 32:36. The psalm prays that very pair of promises. Other voices in Scripture ask the same question of the same God: Jeremiah, 'Why does the way of the wicked prosper?' Jeremiah 12:1, and Habakkuk, 'How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear?' Habakkuk 1:2. Asaph found his answer only when he 'entered God's sanctuary,' Psalm 73:17.

The New Testament takes the psalm up in three ways. Paul quotes verse 11 in 1 Corinthians 3:20, changing 'man' to 'the wise' to make the point about worldly wisdom. Paul and the writer to the Hebrews draw on the theme of Deuteronomy 32:35, Romans 12:19 and Hebrews 10:30, and Hebrews 12:5 to 11 unfolds the beatitude of verse 12 on the Father's discipline. Finally the cry 'How long' is given to the martyrs under the altar, Revelation 6:10, and Jesus answers it with a promise that God 'will promptly carry out justice on their behalf,' Luke 18:8.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted his people to have words for outrage that did not end in either despair or revenge. He hands the wrong to the one person entitled to punish it. Nothing in the psalm tells the hearer to take a sword, file a petition or plot a reprisal; every verb of judgment is aimed at God. That restraint is itself the teaching, for it keeps anger from turning into the thing it condemns.

He also meant to break the spell of the oppressors' confidence. Their claim in verse 7 is a theory of reality, that no one is watching. The poem answers it with an argument, not a shout, and then turns to the faithful and says the way to survive an unjust season is to let God teach you in it. The blessed man of verse 12 is not the one who has escaped trouble but the one who is being instructed in it, and the days of trouble have an end fixed by God, verse 13.

Finally the psalmist was offering a pattern for the worshiper's own testimony. Verses 16 to 19 are not theory. They name a slipping foot, a crowd of anxious thoughts and a hand that held, and invite every reader to find the same in their own story.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records the cry of the wronged and the violence of the wicked; it does not command anyone to share the wicked's ways or the psalmist's wish for destruction as a programme. The cry for vengeance is a prayer, not an instruction to exact it. Paul fixes that reading when he writes 'Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath,' Romans 12:19, quoting the very text this psalm leans on.

The lines that carry over to every generation are the ones that describe God: that He sees and hears, that He disciplines those He loves, and that He will not forsake His heritage. The parts that describe a particular season, the corrupt throne and the bands gathering against the righteous, are to be read as a pattern of what can happen and not as a forecast for every believer. A reader today may rightly pray this psalm about a court, a clinic or a household where the weak are being crushed, and may rightly work for their protection, because the God addressed here defends the fatherless and widow, Deuteronomy 10:18. What the psalm does not allow is the claim that every hardship is a verdict against the sufferer, or every enemy an enemy of God.

debates.question: Does verse 20's 'corrupt throne' refer to a foreign oppressive power or corrupt leadership within Israel itself?

views.label: It refers to corrupt leadership within Israel, using the law itself to oppress the vulnerable
views.case: Verse 20's language of a throne 'devising mischief by decree' points to abuse of legitimate legal authority, matching the prophets' repeated critiques of Israel's own corrupt judges and rulers who exploited widows, foreigners, and orphans under cover of law, Isaiah 10:1-2.

views.label: It refers to a foreign occupying power ruling unjustly over God's people
views.case: The psalm's earlier language of enemies crushing 'Your heritage,' verse 5, may point instead to a foreign ruling power oppressing Israel from outside, a common experience in the exilic and post-exilic periods. The victims in verse 6 include the foreigner, which fits a setting where the victim is a people and not merely a class.

debates.bearing: Either way, the psalm insists that no human throne, whether within Israel or over her, escapes accountability to the LORD, the true Judge of the earth, who will not let injustice committed under any legal cover stand forever.

debates.question: Is the prayer for vengeance in verses 1 to 3 and 23 a fitting prayer for a believer, given Jesus' call to love enemies?

views.label: It is a legitimate prayer that entrusts justice to God
views.case: The psalm asks God, not the worshiper, to act, which is the posture Romans 12:19 commands. Revelation 6:10 puts the same cry in the mouths of the martyrs, and Luke 18:7 has Jesus promising that God will bring about justice for His elect who cry out day and night. Silence before evil would be the stranger response.

views.label: It belongs to the old covenant and is superseded by love of enemies
views.case: Jesus says 'Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,' Matthew 5:44, and on the cross He prayed for His killers, Luke 23:34. On this view the psalm shows what the saints felt before the cross, and Christians are now called to pray for the conversion of oppressors instead.

views.label: Both belong together, and the cross holds them in tension
views.case: Jesus prayed for forgiveness and He is the appointed Judge, John 5:22. God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and wants them to turn, Ezekiel 18:23, yet He will not leave wrong unanswered. The believer may pray for the oppressor's repentance and for the oppression to end, and may leave it to Christ how each is answered.

debates.bearing: The psalm is a model of where anger goes, not a licence for hatred. A Christian reading keeps the cry for justice but prays it in the light of the cross, where justice and mercy were both carried out.

study.originalLanguages:
The opening address is stronger in Hebrew than in English. 'God of vengeance' uses a plural noun, nequmot, so that the phrase reads something like 'God of acts of vengeance,' and it is repeated, which is why the BSB prints it twice. The plural intensifies rather than multiplies: this is full and settled retribution. The verb 'shine forth' in verse 1, from the root yapha, is the verb of God appearing in radiance, used of Him coming from Sinai in Deuteronomy 33:2 and from Zion in Psalm 50:2. The psalmist is praying for a theophany, for God to step into the light of the courtroom.

The rebuke of verse 8 uses two names for fools. The 'senseless,' from the root ba'ar, are the brutish, people who have put themselves in the category of beasts, and the 'fools,' kesil, are the dull who will not learn. Both are wisdom words from Proverbs. In the argument of verse 9 the verbs are carefully chosen: God 'affixed' the ear, a word that means to plant, and 'formed' the eye with the same verb used for the forming of the man in Genesis 2:7. The eye and ear are not accidents of biology; they are the work of a potter.

Verse 12 begins with 'Blessed,' the same word that opens the Psalter, Psalm 1:1, and it is applied to a geber, a man in his strength. The man God disciplines, yasar, is also 'taught,' and what he is taught from is torah, instruction. Discipline in this verse is not punishment but schooling. The same verb appears in verse 10 for God's instruction of the nations, so the teacher who disciplines Israel is also the teacher of the whole world.

In verse 17 the psalmist says that without God he would have lived in 'the abode of silence,' dumah, which is the same word Psalm 115:17 uses of the dead who do not praise the LORD. The fear is not merely death but the end of speech, of prayer and of praise. Verse 19 sets anxiety against consolation with two plural nouns. The 'anxiety' is the plural sar'appim, a word for troubled, restless thoughts that the psalmist also uses in Psalm 139:23 when he asks God to know his 'concerns.' The 'consolation' is tanchumim, comforts. The mind forks into a hundred worries and God answers with more than one comfort.

Finally the decree of verse 20 is choq, the word for a statute, joined to a throne of havvot, ruin or disaster. A law that produces ruin is a contradiction of what law is for.

typology.type: The Judge of the earth who rises to put the world right, verses 1 to 2
typology.fulfillment: Abraham pleaded 'Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?' Genesis 18:25, and the psalmist asks the same Judge to rise. The New Testament names the One through whom He will do it: God 'has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed,' Acts 17:31, and 'the Father judges no one, but has assigned all judgment to the Son,' John 5:22. The pattern is an earthly cry answered in a person. The type falls short because the psalm only asks for the Judge to appear, while the Gospels say the Judge has already come once in weakness and stood before a human court.

typology.type: Innocent blood condemned by a band of the powerful, verse 21
typology.fulfillment: Verse 21 says the wicked 'band together against the righteous and condemn the innocent to death,' and the BSB notes the alternative reading 'condemn innocent blood.' The pattern climaxes in the trial of Jesus. The chief priests and elders conspired against Him, Judas confessed 'I have sinned by betraying innocent blood,' Matthew 27:4, and Pilate washed his hands, saying he was innocent of this man's blood, Matthew 27:24. The correspondence is not a prediction of the passion, but it is the same sin on its largest stage. What makes the cross unique is that God used this very miscarriage of justice for redemption, Acts 2:23-24, which no ordinary unjust verdict does.

typology.type: The disciplined son taught from the law, verse 12
typology.fulfillment: The man whom God teaches is a pattern of the beloved son, and Hebrews takes up the theme in full: 'the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and He chastises every son He receives,' Hebrews 12:6. The escalation in Christ is that He stands inside the pattern, for 'Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered,' Hebrews 5:8. His sufferings were not correction for sin, which is where the type falls short, but they were real schooling in obedience, and they make Him the pioneer of every other disciplined son.

typology.type: The Rock who holds the slipping foot, verses 18 and 22
typology.fulfillment: The foot that slips and is supported by God's loving devotion is a picture of the believer kept by grace. The psalm calls God 'my rock of refuge,' a title the Song of Moses gives Him as 'the Rock, His work is perfect,' Deuteronomy 32:4. In the New Testament the security is entrusted to Christ: 'No one can snatch them out of My hand,' John 10:28, and 'He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion,' Philippians 1:6. The promise is greater in Christ because it rests not on the worshiper's grip but on the Shepherd's. The psalm's image remains limited to one person's experience, and Christ enlarges it to the whole flock.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ most plainly through its first prayer. The psalmist asks the Judge of the earth to rise up and render a reward to the proud, and the New Testament tells us that judgment has been placed in the hands of the Son. 'The Father judges no one, but has assigned all judgment to the Son,' John 5:22, so that the cry of Psalm 94 is not sent into a void but to a named person who will answer it. Paul told the Athenians that God 'has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed,' Acts 17:31, and the proof he gave was the resurrection. The one the courts of earth condemned is the one who will sit over them.

It leads to Christ by contrast and by pattern in the trial of verse 21. The psalm describes a throne that condemns the innocent, and the Gospels show it happening to the one truly innocent man. Jesus told Pilate, 'You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above,' John 19:11. Every line of the psalm's complaint is fulfilled at the cross, and yet the cross becomes the place where the complaint is answered. The apostles' preaching says it in one breath: He was 'delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge,' and killed 'by the hands of the lawless,' yet 'God raised Him from the dead,' Acts 2:23-24. Injustice was not bypassed but used, and then reversed.

He is also the pattern of how to bear such injustice. Peter writes that 'When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23. That is verses 1 and 23 of this psalm lived out: the wrong is handed to the Judge, not repaid by the sufferer. Jesus did the thing the psalm only prays. It is also why Christians can pray Psalm 94 without bitterness.

The beatitude of verse 12 is fulfilled in Him too. He is the Son who learned obedience through what He suffered, Hebrews 5:8, and through whom believers share in the Father's discipline as sons, Hebrews 12:5-11. The seeing God of verse 9 also entered human history and saw the widow's coins, and the oppressed crowds, and the man born blind. His compassion is the eye of the God who formed the eye.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The psalm does not predict Jesus' trial or quote His words, and the 'corrupt throne' is not a code for Pilate. The link is made by the New Testament's own use of the themes, the Judge, the innocent blood, the disciplined son, and not by treating each verse as a hidden picture of the passion.
study.god:
The great claim of this psalm is that God perceives. The oppressors' boast in verse 7, that the LORD does not see, is answered not by an appeal to miracles but by an argument from creation: the God who planted the ear hears and the God who formed the eye sees, verse 9. It is the same God who told Moses in Egypt, 'I have indeed seen the affliction of My people... I have heard them crying out,' Exodus 3:7. To worship Him is to believe that nothing done in a dark room, a closed court or a quiet back street is unobserved.

He is also a knowing God. Verse 10 asks whether the One who teaches man lacks knowledge, and verse 11 says He knows the thoughts of man, that they are futile. Paul quotes that verse to humble the wise, 1 Corinthians 3:20. Human scheming looks like strength from the inside and like vapour from God's side. The psalm does not flatter the powerful by treating them as a real rival to God.

He holds two things together that our instincts keep apart: vengeance and compassion. Deuteronomy 32:35-36 puts them side by side, 'Vengeance is Mine' and 'the LORD will vindicate His people and have compassion on His servants.' The God who avenges is the God who disciplines His own people with a father's purpose, Proverbs 3:12, and who will not forsake them, verse 14. His judgments are not the spasm of an angry deity but the settled work of a righteous one, which is why the psalm can ask for them without asking for chaos.

He is patient, and the psalm does not hide the cost of His patience. The 'How long' of verse 3 is not rebuked. It is written into the hymnbook of Israel. God's delay is real and painful, yet the sure end in verse 13 is fixed, 'until a pit is dug for the wicked,' and the New Testament adds that the delay has a merciful purpose, 'not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance,' 2 Peter 3:9.

He is personally near to the anxious. The language of verses 18 and 19 is tender: a slipping foot, a multitude of thoughts, a hand that steadies and a consolation that delights the soul. The Judge of the earth is also the one who lifts a single trembling person.

For worship the psalm teaches three postures: to protest honestly, to be taught, and to rest. A church that cannot lament has lost half its hymns, and a church that only laments has lost the other half. The psalm ends not on an abstraction but on a relationship, 'The LORD our God,' who is stronghold, rock and refuge.

crossReferences.note: The source of the phrase 'God of vengeance.' Moses's song says 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay' and in the next breath that the LORD will vindicate His people and have compassion on His servants. The psalmist prays both halves: that God will act against the proud, and that He will not forsake His heritage, verse 14.

God's own law against exploiting the foreigner, widow and orphan, with the promise that He will hear their cry. The victims named in verse 6 are exactly the ones the law protected, so the killers are not only criminals but defiers of a word God had spoken in His own voice.

The prophet's 'Woe' against those who enact unjust statutes and make widows their prey is the same charge as verse 20, a throne devising mischief by decree. Both texts say law is meant to shield the weak, and that to turn it against them is to invite the judgment of the true King.

Jeremiah brings the same complaint in a courtroom metaphor, 'Why does the way of the wicked prosper?' and admits that God is righteous even while he contends with Him. Psalm 94 shows how to do what Jeremiah does, to argue with God from inside faith, and not from outside it.

Asaph found the wicked's prosperity troublesome until he 'entered God's sanctuary' and discerned their end. Psalm 94:12-13 gives the same answer, that the man taught by God sees that the wicked have a fixed end, a pit is being dug, and therefore can endure the days of trouble.

Paul quotes verse 11, 'The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are futile,' replacing the psalm's word for man with the wise. He uses it to tell the Corinthians not to boast in human leaders or cleverness, showing how the psalm's attack on the arrogant applies inside the church as well.

Paul tells believers 'leave room for God's wrath' and cites Deuteronomy 32:35. It is the New Testament's commentary on the psalm's posture: the injured do not become their own judges. The psalm's prayer and Paul's command fit together, for the cry for vengeance is precisely how one leaves room for it.

The writer unfolds verse 12's beatitude, telling the weary that the Lord disciplines the one He loves and that discipline 'yields a harvest of righteousness and peace.' The psalm's blessed man, taught from the law in days of trouble, is the pattern of the disciplined child of God.

The martyrs under the altar cry 'How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood?' It is the psalm's third verse lifted into heaven, and it shows the prayer for justice is not a defect in the old covenant but part of the church's own voice until the end.

Jesus answers the 'How long' of the righteous with a parable about a persistent widow, the very kind of person the wicked of verse 6 kill. God 'will promptly carry out justice on their behalf,' and the question is whether the Son of Man will find faith when He comes. It turns the psalm's prayer into a command to keep praying.

Paul announces a day fixed for judging the world by a man God has appointed. It answers verse 2, where the psalmist asks the Judge of the earth to rise, by naming the Judge and giving the proof of His appointment, the resurrection.

Two psalms on, the nations are told that the LORD reigns and will judge in righteousness, and even the fields are told to exult, using the verb the wicked use in 94:3. The exultation of the wicked is taken from them and given to creation, which is where the book of Psalms is heading.

study.oneStory:
The psalm's first question, how a God who made all things well can let the wicked exult, is the question Genesis has already been living with since the first blood hit the ground. 'The voice of your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground,' Genesis 4:10, is the original of the widow's and orphan's cry in Psalm 94:6, and the psalm's 'Judge of the earth' echoes Abraham's bold question 'Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?' Genesis 18:25. Wrong and the demand that it be put right run from the garden on.

Israel was called to be a people in whom this question would be answered in practice. The law at Sinai named the widow, the foreigner and the fatherless as those God would personally defend, Exodus 22:21-24, and Israel was told to remember that they themselves had been foreigners in Egypt. When the nation's own courts turned on the weak, the prophets called it Israel's undoing. This psalm sits at the point where a people who had been oppressed have become oppressors, and only God can set it right.

The Psalter places it as a bridge. Psalm 93 states that the LORD reigns, Psalm 95 calls a chastened people to bow before Him, and in between stands the honest complaint that He does not yet seem to. Book IV teaches that God's kingship is true before it is visible, and that the righteous live in the interval by being taught, held up and comforted.

The interval ends in Christ. He came into the world as an innocent man condemned by a corrupt court, bore the wrong without revenge, and was vindicated by the resurrection. The Father has put all judgment in His hands, and He has promised that His people's cry will not go unheard. The martyrs' 'How long' in Revelation 6:10 shows the church is still praying the psalm.

The new creation is where the psalm ends. In the vision of Revelation 19:1-2 a great multitude cries 'His judgments are true and just,' because He has avenged the blood of His servants. After that there is 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4. The corrupt throne gives way to the throne of God and of the Lamb, from which nothing harmful comes. The God who was once asked to shine forth will be seen, and the silence the psalmist feared, dumah, will be replaced by the sound of people who praise Him.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist ask God to do in verses 1-2?

options.text: Shine forth as the God of vengeance and rise up as Judge of the earth to reward the proud.
options.note: These opening verses are an urgent plea for God to act as the rightful Judge against injustice.

options.text: Remain silent and inactive forever.
options.note: The plea is the opposite, urging God to act decisively, not remain inactive.

options.text: Give the psalmist personal authority to punish his enemies.
options.note: The psalmist appeals to God to act, not to be given personal authority to take vengeance himself.

options.text: Judge the earth with perfect righteousness.
options.note: This is true and closely related, though verses 1-2 specifically call on God as the God of vengeance to shine forth and reward the proud, a more pointed plea than a general statement about judgment.

quiz.q: According to verses 5-7, whom do the wicked oppress, and what do they claim about God?

options.text: They crush the widow, the foreigner, and the fatherless, claiming the LORD does not see.
options.note: These verses name the specific vulnerable groups oppressed and the wicked's false claim of divine blindness.

options.text: They protect the vulnerable and honor God's sight.
options.note: The text describes the opposite: oppression of the vulnerable and denial of God's awareness.

options.text: They oppress only foreign armies, not ordinary people.
options.note: The specific victims named are the widow, foreigner, and fatherless, common people, not armies.

options.text: They boast in arrogant words and consider themselves unaccountable.
options.note: This is true and closely related, verse 4, though the specific claim named in verse 7 is that the LORD does not see or pay heed.

quiz.q: What rebuke does the psalmist give the foolish in verses 8-9?

options.text: That the God who formed the eye and ear surely sees and hears everything.
options.note: These verses argue from God's role as Creator to His full awareness of human deeds.

options.text: That God has no ability to perceive human actions.
options.note: The rebuke argues the opposite: God's Creator status guarantees His full awareness.

options.text: That wisdom is unattainable for anyone.
options.note: The passage calls fools to become wise, implying wisdom is attainable, not impossible.

options.text: That the wicked are foolish for doubting God's awareness.
options.note: This is essentially correct in substance, though the specific argument given in verse 9 reasons from God's role as Creator of the eye and ear to His certain awareness.

options.text: The one whom the LORD disciplines and teaches from His law.
options.note: This verse presents God's loving discipline and instruction as a genuine blessing.

options.text: The one who avoids all correction from God.
options.note: The blessing described is receiving God's discipline and instruction, not avoiding it.

options.text: The one who never experiences any trouble.
options.note: Verse 13 describes relief from days of trouble, implying trouble is present, not absent.

options.text: The one who receives relief during days of trouble.
options.note: This is true and part of the same thought, verse 13, though verse 12 specifically names the blessing as being disciplined and taught from God's law.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's cry for justice find its ultimate answer according to the New Testament?

options.text: God has entrusted all judgment to Jesus Christ the Son.
options.note: John 5:22 shows the Father has given all judgment to the Son, fulfilling this psalm's cry for the rightful Judge to rise up.

options.text: It has no connection to any New Testament teaching.
options.note: The New Testament directly addresses divine judgment and vengeance in relation to Christ.

options.text: It is answered only through human courts and legal systems.
options.note: The psalm looks to God Himself, ultimately fulfilled in Christ, as the true Judge, not merely human legal systems.

options.text: It calls believers to leave vengeance to God rather than avenge themselves.
options.note: This is true, Romans 12:19, and closely related, though the fullest New Testament answer is that the Father has given all judgment specifically to the Son, John 5:22.

questions: The psalmist cries out honestly against injustice rather than staying silent. Is there an injustice in your world right now that you need to bring honestly before God in prayer?
The wicked claim, 'The LORD does not see.' Where might you be tempted to act as though God is not truly aware of what is happening in your life or in the world?
Verse 12 calls God's discipline a blessing. How do you typically respond to correction, whether from God or others, and can you see a difficult season of discipline as ultimately for your good?
The psalmist testifies, 'Your loving devotion, O LORD, supports me,' when his foot was slipping. What is currently causing you to feel unsteady, and how might you lean more fully on God's support?
This psalm's cry for justice is entrusted to Christ, to whom all judgment has been given. How does trusting Jesus as the appointed Judge free you from needing to secure justice on your own?

translationNotes.note: God of vengeance renders a Hebrew phrase describing rightful judicial retribution belonging to God alone, not personal or vindictive revenge.
This verse is directly quoted in 1 Corinthians 3:20, where Paul applies it to the futility of merely human wisdom before God.
Condemn the innocent to death can also be rendered condemn innocent blood, emphasizing the severity of judicial injustice the psalm protests.
